newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia privatisation to initiate further reforms.
newsitem.headline: Serbia privatisation to initiate further reforms.

text.p: Serbia will adopt its new draft privatisation law by the end of May , clearing the path to further reforms, Serbian Minister for Economic and Ownership Transformation Milan Beko said on Wednesday.
Privatisation was also seen attracting more foreign participation in an economy shattered by almost four years of war-related sanctions.

"Serbia wants to become an open market economy, but to make it happen we must complete a legal framework. The privatisation law was one of the very important legal documents for an economic transition that was missing," Beko told Reuters.
The process will be gradual and its pace will depend on the country's return to world financial institutions, he said.
Beko insisted there was a strong political will for reforms. "There is an absolute political consensus on reforms and the atmosphere is very good. There are no obstacles."
The first Serbian privatisation minister was confident the offered privatisation concept would create a more favourable environment in Serbia and improve performance of local firms.

"The privatisation law is a good reform law, bringing more democracy into the economy and making clear who owns what. It will create nearly four million shareholders. But the utmost aim is to raise the efficiency of privatised companies," he said.

Along with privatisation, Serbia was readying a new law granting concessions in infrastructure, forestry, waterways and a lottery and will offer mining rights to investors. They can choose between direct investment and debt-for-equity swaps.
But in privatising state companies of special interest, Serbia will seek strategic partners.
"The investors will be offered heavy incentives, such as a 30 percent discount if buying more than 40 percent stake of a company," Beko said.
Analysts welcomed the new Serbian privatisation law as a sign of good will by the ruling Socialists to reform the economy frequently referred to as the last communist stronghold in Europe.
But they also warned privatisation could fail for relying heavily on the participation of impoverished workers.
"It's good that Serbia will privatise, but with penniless workers you could hardly call this a socially fair concept," said a Western diplomat, speaking under condition of anonymity.
By law, employees and pensioners are entitled to any number of shares, but a maximum of 20,000 German marks worth of companies' stock is eligible for discounts.

"The moment workers subscribe, but only within one year of the share issue, they get 70 percent of their shares free. They will also enjoy a 20 percent basic discount plus one percent discount for each year of service," Beko said.
A government economist said the Serbian constitution did not allow the handing over of companies' stock free to the population. "It takes at least two years to amend the constitution."
Beko said trade in shares acquired free of charge through an incentives package will not be allowed for two years.

"We are aware of the poverty. We banned any trade in those shares for two years because we want to prevent workers from selling. After two years we expect the purchasing power to pick up and the share value to increase," Beko said.
A source close to the government said the privatisation itself was not expected to fill in cash-strapped state coffers. "Capital will start flowing in because of privatisation."
The government signalled it would allow old hard currency savings, frozen in 1991, to be used for buying shares.
Beko said those savings will be used to purchase shares in the second stage of privatisation from the Serbian Share Fund.
"There was an idea to activate those deposits in the first round of privatisation, with an insider shareholder scheme, but we realised this would complicate matters.

Privatisation receipts go to three state funds, but those funds need no paper based on hard currency savings. They need cash to improve their financial situation," Beko said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
